# Where to Next: Open Problems {#sec-open-problems}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A book about a research engine has to end with a chapter about
what is *not* yet built. The vision in Chapter 1 is ambitious; the
implementation we have walked through is large but incomplete.
The honest place to close is where the team is going next.

This chapter inventories the open problems. They are drawn from
the in-tree design documents, the CLAUDE.md notes, and the gaps
this book has flagged in earlier chapters. None of them is
"trivial cleanup"; each is the subject of active research.

---

## 22.1 What's left in the distributed story {#sec-distributed-future}

The first draft of this chapter named "moving from single-node to
distributed" as the single biggest open problem. That description
was wrong — distribution had landed on `origin/main` (Chapter 19).
The open-problem list got *longer*, not shorter, as the
all-encompassing item resolved into several finer ones.

**Cost-model calibration for the ILP planner.** The current
distributed planner weights network bandwidth and per-worker
load, but the weights are still hand-tuned. Real workloads
need hardware-affinity-aware weighting (a GPU operator's cost
differs from a CPU operator's) and the ILP solver needs to
scale to topologies of hundreds of workers, not the dozens
currently exercised in tests.

**Failure recovery and checkpointing.** A worker crash today
fails the query and requires re-submission. The catalog
infrastructure is in place to make recovery possible; the
actual checkpoint-and-replay machinery is the next major work
item. We treat this as its own sub-problem in @sec-checkpointing.

**Adaptive operator re-placement.** Topology changes — a
vehicle drives through a tunnel, an edge gateway
disconnects — currently fail the query. Re-placing operators
when the topology shifts without losing in-flight state is the
deepest research problem on the engine's roadmap.

**Heterogeneous-hardware-aware placement.** The planner treats
workers as comparably capable. Once the GPU/TPU backends
mature (@sec-accelerators), the planner needs to know that
"this worker has a GPU" and "this operator wants a GPU." The
placement framework is ready; the cost model is not yet
calibrated for it.

**Coordinator merge.** As of May 2026, the Rust coordinator on
the `ys-coordinator-integration` branch has not yet merged to
`main`. Bringing it across — and the policy work it implies
(failover, leader election, coordinator HA) — is on the
critical path.

---

## 22.2 Multi-query optimisation {#sec-multi-query}

The optimiser today (Chapter 9) optimises one query at a time.
For workloads with hundreds of overlapping queries — say, hundreds
of dashboards each computing a slightly different aggregation
over the same input — there is significant opportunity to share
work *across* queries.

The classical approach is **multi-query optimisation** [@mqo-roy]:
identify common subexpressions across queries, share their
computation. A streaming variant is harder than the batch case
because the queries arrive at different times and may have
different windowing requirements, but the savings can be large.

NebulaStream's optimiser does not do this today. It would be a
substantial extension — a new phase that operates on a *set of
queries* rather than a single query, plus runtime changes to
share state structures between queries.

---

## 22.3 In-network processing {#sec-in-network}

The vision statement promises "in-network processing" — pushing
operators close to data sources to reduce the volume of data
crossing the network. Implemented to its logical end, this
means running selections and projections on the source's edge
device, not the cloud worker.

What is needed:

- **An edge runtime.** A NebulaStream runtime light enough for
  edge gateways or even sensor microcontrollers. This is not the
  current `nes-single-node-worker` (too heavyweight); it is a
  stripped-down sibling that can run a subset of operators in a
  small footprint.
- **Cost-aware operator placement.** A model of network bandwidth
  cost so the optimiser can decide which operators to push
  edge-ward.
- **Coordination across the cloud-edge boundary.** State
  synchronisation when an operator moves; reasoning about
  watermark progress when some upstream is on a flaky network.

The DIMA group has published research papers on each of these;
the implementation is partial.

---

## 22.4 Heterogeneous accelerators (GPU, TPU, FPGA) {#sec-accelerators}

Chapter 19 mentioned that GPU support exists as a research
prototype outside the main tree, with TPU and FPGA support as
aspirations. The infrastructure to *add* these — Nautilus's MLIR
backend (Chapter 12) and the `pmr::memory_resource` extension
(Chapter 4) — is in place; the backends themselves are work in
progress.

Two distinct sub-problems:

- **Compiling operators to non-CPU targets.** MLIR has dialects
  for SPIR-V (GPU), and prototype lowering passes from
  Nautilus's IR to those dialects exist. Productionising them
  requires substantial QA and likely more research.
- **Runtime orchestration of heterogeneous hardware.** The
  scheduler today does not know that thread A is on a GPU; it
  treats all worker threads as equivalent. Heterogeneous-aware
  scheduling needs new abstractions.

This is a long-term research direction; expect incremental
progress, not a single big release.

---

## 22.5 Adaptive runtime: changing plans on the fly {#sec-adaptive}

The fifth pillar in the README is "Adaptive Resource
Management — Reacts to topology or workload changes without
interrupting queries." Today the engine's plan is fixed at query
compile time; adapting to changing conditions requires stopping
and restarting the query.

What "adaptive" might mean concretely:

- **Re-optimisation on workload shift.** A join whose hash side
  was sized for 1 million rows now sees 100 million rows; the
  optimiser should be able to swap to a different join algorithm
  mid-flight.
- **Operator migration.** An operator running on worker X
  becomes too loaded; the engine moves it to worker Y without
  losing state or data.
- **Schema evolution.** A source's schema changes (a field is
  added). Queries adapt without re-submission.

Each is hard. Adaptive runtimes are an active research area;
[@adaptive-streaming] is a survey of the state of the art.
NebulaStream has not yet committed to a specific adaptive
mechanism; the design space is open.

---

## 22.6 Late-data side outputs {#sec-late-data}

A smaller but practically important gap. NebulaStream today
silently drops tuples whose event time is older than the most
recently fired window (Chapter 7). Flink, by contrast, supports
*late-data side outputs* — a separate output stream where dropped
tuples can be inspected and, if appropriate, re-incorporated.

Adding side outputs to NebulaStream is mostly an engineering
problem (the watermark and slice machinery is already
slice-aware), but it is a useful feature that is currently
absent.

---

## 22.7 Persistent state and checkpointing {#sec-checkpointing}

Chapter 16's discussion of stateful operators noted that
NebulaStream's state is in-memory only; on a worker crash, all
state is lost. Production streaming engines almost universally
support **checkpointing** — periodic snapshots of state to
durable storage that can be replayed after a crash to resume the
query at the most recent checkpoint.

Adding checkpointing requires:

- A serialisation format for hash maps and PagedVectors.
- A coordination protocol that briefly pauses tuple processing
  long enough to take a consistent snapshot (the Chandy-Lamport
  algorithm [@chandy-lamport] in some adapted form).
- A storage abstraction for the snapshots — local filesystem,
  S3, etc.
- A recovery path that reads the snapshot and brings up the
  query at the right point in its history.

This is a substantial undertaking and partly intersects with the
distributed-execution work — checkpointing is more useful when
distribution is the default.

---

## 22.8 The list goes on {#sec-list-goes-on}

There is more. Briefly:

- **Streaming SQL extensions** — `MATCH_RECOGNIZE` for pattern
  detection, more sophisticated session-window definitions.
- **More plugin extension points** — user-defined functions,
  user-defined window types, user-defined aggregations.
- **Better observability** — structured query plans visualised
  in real time; predictive alerts on performance regressions.
- **Cost-based optimisation** — when the rule-based optimiser of
  Chapter 9 stops being enough.
- **Approximate-query support** — sketches, count-min, HyperLogLog
  as first-class operators.

Each of these would expand the engine's capability surface; none
is a single-PR change.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch22-summary}

NebulaStream is a research engine with a substantial implementation
behind it and a substantial implementation ahead. The largest open
problem is full distributed execution (a QueryManager,
inter-worker communication, fault recovery), with multi-query
optimisation, in-network processing, accelerator backends,
adaptive runtime, late-data side outputs, and checkpointing
following close behind. The vision in Chapter 1 maps cleanly onto
this list of work; the gap between vision and implementation is
the engine's research agenda.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch22-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 22.1: read a design document"}
Pick one of the recently dated design documents in
`docs/design/`. Read it carefully. What problem is it solving?
What is the proposed solution? Do you agree with the trade-offs?
Write a one-page critique.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 22.2: implement a tiny extension"}
Pick the smallest item from the open-problem list — perhaps
late-data side outputs — and sketch how you would implement it.
Where in the code would you start? What new types would you
introduce? What existing code would you need to change?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 22.3: write the next book"}
Of the items in this chapter, several would warrant their own
book-length treatment. Identify two and outline what such a
book would cover. The most likely candidates: distributed
execution (a follow-on book once the QueryManager lands), and
adaptive runtime (a research-monograph book covering the
current literature plus NebulaStream's eventual approach).
:::
